extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, practising chymists, and learned readers interested in the foundations and methods of chymistry (17th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing chymical (chemical) writings, experiments, and claims about elemental principles — focusing on clarity of exposition, experimental sufficiency, and correct inference about elementarity from operations like distillation and calcination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and intelligibility of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers teaching general principles should make their notions intelligible rather than darken them with mystical terms and ambiguous phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mystification: 'in such Speculative Enquiries, where the naked Knowledge of the Truth is the thing Principally aim'd at, what does he teach me worth thanks that does not, if he can, make his Notion intelligible to me, but by Mystical Termes, and Ambiguous Phrases darkens what he should clear up.' Anti-pattern: writing obscurely to appear venerable or to conceal weakness. Prefer plain, clear teaching when the aim is to communicate natural-philosophical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable and consistent use of names (terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not 'play with Names at pleasure' — avoid assigning the same name to diverse things or many names to the same thing without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology must be tied to described properties. The text warns that eminent writers call the same substance 'sometimes the Sulphur, and Sometimes the Mercury of a Body.' Anti-pattern: inventing or reassigning names capriciously; justification for neologisms must be given and consistent with descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equivocal and canting style to conceal weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use hard words and equivocal expressions to make knowledge seem precious or to hide ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage criticises authors who write obscurely either to be admired or to conceal that their notions are unclear: 'they will find the Major part of Knowing Men so vain... to conclude, that it is rather the Writers fault then their own.' Good practice: write plainly unless a genuine reason exists to conceal specific operational secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear descriptions when naming supposed principles
rubrics_metrics.description: If you call a substance an elemental principle (e.g., Sulphur), you must describe its properties so that others can test and judge the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once an author defines Sulphur as 'a Primogeneal and simple Body, Inflamable, Odorous, &c.' they cannot then claim unrelated bodies are that Sulphur. Inconsistent attribution (e.g., 'an Incombustible Sulphur') is shown as an absurdity. Guidance: definitions should constrain legitimate identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical demonstration and reproducible experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about principles or substances should be supported by experiments that others can reproduce and examine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses the need for experiments and offers examples (distillation mixtures, distilling olive oil with sal circulatum, the author's own retort experiments producing brimstone) while cautioning against relying solely on unverified reports (Helmont). Anti-pattern: asserting facts based only on cant or authority without experimental detail or reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between having experimental skill and giving a philosophical account
rubrics_metrics.description: Being able to perform operations (make experiments) is different from being able to explain them philosophically; both capacities are relevant and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As noted: 'there is great Difference betwixt the being able to make Experiments, and the being able to give a Philosophical Account of them.' Good practice: pair experimental demonstrations with coherent explanation, but judge each independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer elementarity merely because a substance is separable by fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances obtained by heating or distillation are not necessarily simple elements; many may be compounded or altered by the fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple arguments: (a) Fire can produce new mixtures or alter textures, (b) substances may be compounded by the fire or pick up particles from the apparatus (glass), (c) examples like soot, vitrification of ashes, and the author's distillation producing brimstone from vitriol+turpentine show separability does not imply elementarity. Guidance: require further analysis beyond mere separability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider that heat/fire can both resolve and compound matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of fire is not purely decompositional; it may also combine parts into new compounds or alter dispositions to produce new qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: soot formation from smoke, ashes becoming glass, camphor being raised in stoppered vessels, formation of volatile salts and oily parts by heating. Anti-pattern: assuming thermal operations only reverse composition; instead investigate possible recombination or generation of new substances by heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate contamination and apparatus effects (e.g., interaction with glass, fire corpuscles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider that apparatus and the fire itself may contribute to new products (e.g., corpuscles of fire associating with body particles or glass porosity allowing ingress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author conjectures swarms of fiery corpuscles entering glass pores and associating with the mixt body, and warns that products could be due to such interactions. Good practice: control for vessel-material effects and consider alternative sources for observed products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about relying on single-method analyses (distillation) for classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysing mixtures only by one operation (such as distillation) can mislead about the components; different preparative methods may yield different products or show compound nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mixing vitriol, sal ammoniac, saltpetre and distilling gives a new liquor not equal to the known spirits; Helmont's sal circulatum yielding different oils from the same starting material. Guidance: use multiple complementary methods and further analysis to establish compositional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide procedural detail and allow others to examine your preparations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting experiments or preparations, include sufficient detail that others can examine, repeat, and analyze the products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author offers to let readers examine samples (e.g., brimstone obtained from his retort) and criticises obscurely intimated processes. Good practice: document steps, reagents, vessel types, and observations; avoid purely anecdotal reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate primary and higher-order mixtures; expect nested compounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some concretes may be composed of ingredients that themselves are compounded (primary, secondary, tertiary mixts), so decomposition may reveal further mixtures rather than elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text outlines Prima Mista, Mista Primaria and secondary mixtures that can lead onward — e.g., native cinnabar containing coarser part, combustible sulphur, running mercury. Guidance: do not assume a finite small set of elements; consider hierarchical composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing from authorities or singular anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Take unverified reports (e.g., Helmont's claims) cautiously and do not make strong theoretical claims based primarily on an authority's obscure description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author sometimes accepts Helmont's observations provisionally but refrains from insisting on them without means to experiment. Good practice: test reported phenomena when possible and remain tentative about claims lacking replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link names to observable qualities but verify underlying nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming by qualities (inflamability → 'sulphur', dissolvability → 'salt', fixedness → 'earth', volatility → 'mercury') is common but insufficient; verify whether those qualities reflect simple elemental nature or altered/disposed states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage warns that qualities might be produced by texture or fire rather than indicate elemental identity (e.g., glass that is dry, fixt, indissoluble yet clearly a mixt body). Guidance: use observed properties as clues but perform deeper analyses before inferring elemental status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for transformations induced by reagents or circulations (e.g., sal circulatum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that reagents and circulations (processing agents) can change a substance into other sorts (e.g., sal circulatum converting olive oil into a different oil or wine yielding different spirits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helmont's cited experiments: digesting olive oil with sal circulatum yields a sweet oil distinct from distilled oil. Guidance: when substances are prepared with added agents, consider that the agent may create new kinds of products rather than merely extract pre-existing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish natural from artificial productions but do not assume sharp boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: When labeling a product as natural or artificial, examine whether the effect depends on artisan design or on natural agents (fire, water) acting in their own natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that many chymical productions may be produced whether intended by the artificer or not, and that the fire is as natural an agent as seed. Guidance: when judging products, consider whether they are results of natural agent interaction or artful contrivance and avoid categorical exclusion without analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to alternative explanations and multiple hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting experimental outcomes, propose and weigh alternative hypotheses (e.g., new compound formation, separation of pre-existing parts, apparatus contribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the text the author offers multiple plausible readings of his retort brimstone result (real sulphur formed, vitriol being compounded, or transmutation by interaction). Good practice: present competing interpretations and design experiments to discriminate among them.
